source: I had not been seated very long ere a man of a certain venerable robustness entered; immediately as the storm-pelted door flew back upon admitting him, a quick regardful eyeing of him by all the congregation, sufficiently attested that this fine old man was the chaplain. Yes, it was the famous Father Mapple, so called by the whalemen, among whom he was a very great favourite. He had been a sailor and a harpooneer in his youth, but for many years past had dedicated his life to the ministry. At the time I now write of, Father Mapple was in the hardy winter of a healthy old age; that sort of old age which seems merging into a second flowering youth, for among all the fissures of his wrinkles, there shone certain mild gleams of a newly developing bloom—the spring verdure peeping forth even beneath February’s snow. No one having previously heard his history, could for the first time behold Father Mapple without the utmost interest, because there were certain engrafted clerical peculiarities about him, imputable to that adventurous maritime life he had led. When he entered I observed that he carried no umbrella, and certainly had not come in his carriage, for his tarpaulin hat ran down with melting sleet, and his great pilot cloth jacket seemed almost to drag him to the floor with the weight of the water it had absorbed. However, hat and coat and overshoes were one by one removed, and hung up in a little space in an adjacent corner; when, arrayed in a decent suit, he quietly approached the pulpit.

Like most old fashioned pulpits, it was a very lofty one, and since a regular stairs to such a height would, by its long angle with the floor, seriously contract the already small area of the chapel, the architect, it seemed, had acted upon the hint of Father Mapple, and finished the pulpit without a stairs, substituting a perpendicular side ladder, like those used in mounting a ship from a boat at sea. The wife of a whaling captain had provided the chapel with a handsome pair of red worsted man-ropes for this ladder, which, being itself nicely headed, and stained with a mahogany colour, the whole contrivance, considering what manner of chapel it was, seemed by no means in bad taste. Halting for an instant at the foot of the ladder, and with both hands grasping the ornamental knobs of the man-ropes, Father Mapple cast a look upwards, and then with a truly sailor-like but still reverential dexterity, hand over hand, mounted the steps as if ascending the main-top of his vessel.

The perpendicular parts of this side ladder, as is usually the case with swinging ones, were of cloth-covered rope, only the rounds were of wood, so that at every step there was a joint. At my first glimpse of the pulpit, it had not escaped me that however convenient for a ship, these joints in the present instance seemed unnecessary. For I was not prepared to see Father Mapple after gaining the height, slowly turn round, and stooping over the pulpit, deliberately drag up the ladder step by step, till the whole was deposited within, leaving him impregnable in his little Quebec.

I pondered some time without fully comprehending the reason for this. Father Mapple enjoyed such a wide reputation for sincerity and sanctity, that I could not suspect him of courting notoriety by any mere tricks of the stage. No, thought I, there must be some sober reason for this thing; furthermore, it must symbolize something unseen. Can it be, then, that by that act of physical isolation, he signifies his spiritual withdrawal for the time, from all outward worldly ties and connexions? Yes, for replenished with the meat and wine of the word, to the faithful man of God, this pulpit, I see, is a self-containing stronghold—a lofty Ehrenbreitstein, with a perennial well of water within the walls.

But the side ladder was not the only strange feature of the place, borrowed from the chaplain’s former sea-farings. Between the marble cenotaphs on either hand of the pulpit, the wall which formed its back was adorned with a large painting representing a gallant ship beating against a terrible storm off a lee coast of black rocks and snowy breakers. But high above the flying scud and dark-rolling clouds, there floated a little isle of sunlight, from which beamed forth an angel’s face; and this bright face shed a distinct spot of radiance upon the ship’s tossed deck, something like that silver plate now inserted into the Victory’s plank where Nelson fell. “Ah, noble ship,” the angel seemed to say, “beat on, beat on, thou noble ship, and bear a hardy helm; for lo! the sun is breaking through; the clouds are rolling off—serenest azure is at hand.”

Nor was the pulpit itself without a trace of the same sea-taste that had achieved the ladder and the picture. Its panelled front was in the likeness of a ship’s bluff bows, and the Holy Bible rested on a projecting piece of scroll work, fashioned after a ship’s fiddle-headed beak.

What could be more full of meaning?—for the pulpit is ever this earth’s foremost part; all the rest comes in its rear; the pulpit leads the world. From thence it is the storm of God’s quick wrath is first descried, and the bow must bear the earliest brunt. From thence it is the God of breezes fair or foul is first invoked for favourable winds. Yes, the world’s a ship on its passage out, and not a voyage complete; and the pulpit is its prow.

paragraphs: I had not been sitting very long before a man of a certain venerable robustness came in. The moment the storm-pelted door flew back to admit him, the whole congregation's quick, respectful eyeing of him was enough to show that this fine old man was the chaplain. Yes, it was the famous Father Mapple, as the whalemen called him, among whom he was a very great favorite. He had been a sailor and a harpooner in his youth, but for many years past had dedicated his life to the ministry. modern_da.title: Kapitel 8 — Prædikestolen
paragraphs: Jeg havde ikke siddet længe, før en mand med en vis ærværdig kraft kom ind. I det øjeblik, den stormpiskede dør fløj op for at lukke ham ind, var det nok at se, hvordan hele menigheden hurtigt og respektfuldt kiggede på ham, til at vise, at denne fine gamle mand var præsten. Ja, det var den berømte Father Mapple, som hvalfangerne kaldte ham, og som var en meget stor favorit blandt dem. Han havde været sømand og harpuner i sin ungdom, men havde i mange år helliget sit liv til præstegerningen. På det tidspunkt, jeg skriver om, var Father Mapple i en sund alderdoms sejlivede vinter — den slags alderdom, der synes at gå over i en anden, blomstrende ungdom, for blandt alle rynkernes furer skinnede der milde glimt af en nyvoksende blomstring, som det grønne forår, der titter frem selv under februars sne. Ingen, der ikke på forhånd havde hørt hans historie, kunne se Father Mapple første gang uden den største interesse, for der var nogle præstelige særheder podet på ham, på grund af det eventyrlige liv til søs, han havde ført. Da han kom ind, lagde jeg mærke til, at han ikke bar paraply og bestemt ikke var kommet i vogn, for hans tjærehat dryppede af smeltende slud, og hans store lodsfrakke syntes næsten at trække ham til gulvet med al den vægt af vand, den havde suget til sig. Men hat og frakke og overtræksstøvler blev taget af én for én og hængt op i en lille plads i et hjørne i nærheden. Og så, klædt i et anstændigt tøj, gik han stille hen mod prædikestolen.

Som de fleste gammeldags prædikestole var den meget høj, og da en almindelig trappe til sådan en højde med sin lange skråning hen over gulvet ville have gjort kapellets i forvejen lille gulvplads endnu mindre, havde arkitekten, så det så ud, fulgt et vink fra Father Mapple og gjort prædikestolen færdig uden trappe. I stedet havde han sat en lodret sidestige, ligesom dem man bruger til at kravle om bord på et skib fra en båd på åbent hav. En hvalfangerkaptajns hustru havde skænket kapellet et smukt par røde rebhåndlister af uld til denne stige, som selv var pænt forsynet med knopper og bejdset i en mahognifarve. Når man tænkte på, hvilken slags kapel det var, syntes hele indretningen på ingen måde at være i dårlig smag. Father Mapple standsede et øjeblik ved foden af stigen med begge hænder om rebhåndlisternes pyntelige knopper, kastede et blik opad, og med en virkelig sømandsagtig, men stadig ærbødig behændighed steg han hånd over hånd op ad trinene, som om han kravlede op til stormærset på sit skib.

Sidestigens lodrette sider var, som det som regel er med hængende stiger, lavet af tøjklædt reb, og kun trinene var af træ, så der var et led ved hvert trin. Da jeg første gang fik øje på prædikestolen, havde jeg lagt mærke til, at hvor bekvemme disse led end kunne være på et skib, syntes de her at være unødvendige. For jeg var ikke forberedt på at se Father Mapple, da han nåede toppen, langsomt dreje sig om, bøje sig over prædikestolen og med vilje hale stigen op trin for trin, til det hele lå stuvet væk indeni og lod ham være uindtagelig i sit lille Quebec.

Jeg grublede længe uden helt at forstå grunden til det. Father Mapple havde så udbredt et ry for oprigtighed og hellighed, at jeg ikke kunne mistænke ham for at jage opmærksomhed ved blotte teaterkneb. Nej, tænkte jeg, der må være en alvorlig grund til dette, og hvad mere er, det må symbolisere noget usynligt. Kan det da være, at han med denne fysiske afsondring viser sin åndelige tilbagetrækning for en tid fra alle ydre, verdslige bånd og forbindelser? Ja, for den troende Guds mand, der er mættet af ordets kød og vin, er denne prædikestol, ser jeg, en selvforsynende fæstning — et højt Ehrenbreitstein med en aldrig svigtende brønd inden for sine mure.

Men sidestigen var ikke det eneste mærkelige ved stedet, der var lånt fra præstens tidligere liv til søs. Mellem marmorkenotaferne på hver side af prædikestolen var væggen bag den prydet med et stort maleri af et tappert skib, der kæmpede sig frem mod en frygtelig storm ud for en lækyst af sorte klipper og snehvide brændinger. Men højt over det flyvende skumsprøjt og de mørke, rullende skyer svævede en lille ø af sollys, hvorfra et engleansigt strålede ud. Og dette lyse ansigt kastede en tydelig plet af glans på skibets omtumlede dæk, noget i retning af den sølvplade, der nu er sat ind i Victorys planker, dér hvor Nelson faldt. »Ak, ædle skib,« syntes englen at sige, »slå dig frem, slå dig frem, du ædle skib, og hold roret hårdt; for se! Solen bryder igennem, skyerne trækker bort — det mest rolige blå er nær.«

Selve prædikestolen bar også spor af den samme sømandssmag, som havde skabt stigen og maleriet. Dens panelerede front var formet som et skibs brede bov, og den hellige Bibel lå på et fremspringende stykke snirkelværk, formet efter et skibs fiolhovedformede snabel.

Hvad kunne være mere fuldt af betydning? For prædikestolen er altid denne jords forreste del; alt det øvrige kommer bagefter; prædikestolen fører verden. Derfra opdager man først stormen af Guds hastige vrede, og stævnen må tage det første stød. Derfra påkalder man først Gud, der råder over gunstige eller ugunstige vinde, om gode vinde. Ja, verden er et skib på udrejse og ikke en fuldført rejse; og prædikestolen er dens forstavn.
